articles.title: Who is Earl Spencer, the man at the center of the latest royal saga?
articles.summary: When Charles Spencer delivered his powerful eulogy for the late Princess Diana, he pledged to protect her sons – whom he referred to as “blood family” – from the anguish that regularly drove his sister “to tearful despair.”
articles.body: When Earl Charles Spencer delivered his powerful eulogy for the late Princess Diana, he pledged to protect her sons – whom he referred to as “blood family” – from the anguish that regularly drove his sister “to tearful despair.” Nearly 30 years on, claims made in his new book risk, as one British newspaper put it, plunging a “dagger into the heart” of those two sons. Spencer claims his former brother-in-law – now King Charles – launched into a “stream of anger” over the phone following Diana’s death, after Spencer argued she would not have wanted William and Harry to take part in her funeral procession, according to excerpts published this week. The King is also accused of saying, “we’ll forget her soon enough” – a claim Buckingham Palace has firmly rejected. Some British media outlets and royal commentators have questioned the purpose of dragging up the past, while others have defended Spencer, saying his book shows he was prioritizing family over royal tradition. Who is Earl Spencer? Charles Spencer was born in London on May 20, 1964, into a prominent British aristocratic family with links to the modern-day royal clan. The late Queen Elizabeth II was his godmother. In 1508, the family purchased the Althorp estate in West Northamptonshire, England, around two and a half hours drive north of London, where their ancestral seat remains to this day. Spencer was educated at Eton, the prestigious school located in the English county of Berkshire, a stone’s throw from Windsor Castle. He then attended Magdalen College at the University of Oxford, where he studied modern history, according to his website. Later, Spencer worked as a journalist, including spending a decade at the American TV network NBC News from 1986 as an on-air correspondent. He has written several books, including titles exploring his own family’s past, as well as books about royal figures such as Charles II. He has five daughters and two sons from his first three marriages, according to his website. What was his relationship with Diana like? Diana and Spencer – who were aged less than three years apart – were very close as children, growing up at Althorp House, their leafy stately home in West Northamptonshire. Spencer remembers their early years fondly and says the pair spent a significant amount of time together, particularly during their parent’s divorce. But their relationship, as with many siblings, wasn’t without its squabbles. Fractures between the pair were documented in a series of letters revealed during the 2002 theft trial of Diana’s former butler. The Telegraph, which reported on the trial, said Diana’s request for a home in the “Garden House” on the family estate following her separation from then-Prince Charles was initially accepted but later turned down by Spencer who suggested alternative properties on the grounds. Another letter cited in the trial referred to a phone call between the siblings in which Diana hung up on her brother. Despite this upset, Spencer delivered an emotional eulogy in 1997 which lauded Diana as the “very essence of compassion, of duty, of style, of beauty.” In the speech, he reminisced about their childhood days when Diana “mothered me as a baby, fought with me at school and endured those long train journeys between our parents’ homes with me at weekends.” He strongly rebuked the British press for their treatment of his sister whom Spencer called the “most hunted person of the modern age.” The eulogy led to applause both in the church and among crowds listening outside. Is he friendly with the British royal family? Spencer held warm feelings towards Charles shortly after the then-Prince of Wales and Diana met at Althorp House in 1977. “He was perfectly pleasant and charming. So, I was quite relaxed about it really,” Spencer told CNN in 1999, speaking about the couple’s marriage plans. “The fact that it was Prince Charles was obviously extraordinary, but otherwise I just, I was more interested in my exams and playing my sports at school.” But that relationship has suffered a very public demise in recent days. A war of words kicked off on Wednesday after Spencer said his former brother-in-law told him days after Diana’s death that she would soon be forgotten, according to an extract published by the Daily Mail from Spencer’s forthcoming book. Buckingham Palace issued a rare rebuttal to Spencer’s claim, saying “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss.” Charles’ alleged comments had not previously been reported. In the 1999 interview, Spencer told CNN that Charles was “perfectly polite” on the day of the funeral. “We all caught the train from London together to go to the burial at my family home, and nothing nasty has ever been said about it by him to me,” Spencer said. Some commentators have noted the impact such revelations could have on Princes William and Harry as they navigate their own rocky relationship, particularly following the surprise return of the Sussexes (who are known to maintain close relations with the Spencer family.) Earlier this year, Harry and Meghan, alongside their children, visited their mother’s ancestral home where she is buried on a small island closed to the public. Also in 2024, when Harry made a brief return to the UK for the 10th anniversary for his Invictus Games, he was supported by several members of the Spencer family who attended the celebration. Harry was seen chatting with his aunt, Lady Jane Fellowes who was seated directly behind him along with his uncle, before the event got underway. The latest public clash between the Spencers and Windsors is therefore a test of alliances for the British royal clan. Many would have hoped the return of the Sussexes could mark a fresh start for the family. Instead, new fractures appear to be developing.

articles.title: Law professor's killer stalked him 'like a shark circling' before ex-mother-in-law's murder-for-hire ambush
articles.summary: Donna Adelson and Charlie Adelson were both sentenced to life in prison for the murder-for-hire plot that killed Dan Markel over a custody dispute.
articles.body: After leaving the gym, Dan Markel drove home expecting an ordinary day. Instead, his killer was waiting for him. As he arrived home, the prominent Florida State University law professor was talking on the phone with music teacher Stewart Schlazer about school options for his children. Then the conversation took a terrifying turn. "Can you please hold on a second? There's an unfamiliar person in my driveway," Markel said. SLAIN DAD'S DAUGHTER KNEW ‘BLACK SWAN’ EX-BALLERINA SHOT HIM AFTER ONE CALL: 'SHE KILLED HIM, DIDN'T SHE?' Seconds later, Schlazer heard what he described as "a loud boom." "There are really eerie parts of those final hours," producer Lily Fletcher told Fox News Digital. "You look at the CCTV footage, and it's a normal day. Dan dropped off the kids at school, he's gone to work out at the gym, and then there's a Prius driving around the gym car park. It never stops. It's clearly waiting for him." "It's always reminded me of a shark circling," Fletcher said. "There was something just so sinister and eerie during such a mundane part of his day, just going to the gym. That really stayed with me. That's a really chilling part, just watching that footage." Markel was shot in the head while sitting in his car in the garage of his Tallahassee, Florida, home on July 18, 2014. The 41-year-old died the following day. The case is the subject of a new true crime docuseries from ABC News Studios, "Welcome to the Family: The Murder of Dan Markel," now streaming on Hulu. It features exclusive interviews, including with FBI agent Pat Sanford and a recorded conversation with Rob Adelson, the oldest Adelson son, who testified against his mother, Donna Adelson, at her trial. It largely follows the prosecution's investigation and trial evidence, while also including testimony and recordings introduced during court proceedings. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Markel married Wendi Adelson in 2006 after the two met online. The docuseries depicts prosecutors' theory that Wendi's mother, Donna, was a dominating, controlling figure in their lives with strong opinions about her daughter's choices. Wendi later said the couple's marriage fell apart after they had two sons, Benjamin and Lincoln. Their contentious divorce in 2013 centered on one question: where the boys would grow up. Wendi fought to move them to South Florida to be near her family, while Markel pressed to keep them in Tallahassee, where the parents shared custody. According to the docuseries, Donna was furious after the relocation request was denied. Prosecutors said the custody dispute became the catalyst for a murder-for-hire plot that would take years to unravel. They argued at trial that Donna helped orchestrate Markel’s killing after he stood in the way of letting her daughter and two young grandsons make the move south. They also revealed that her son Charlie Adelson arranged for Markel's killing through his then-girlfriend, Katherine Magbanua, who connected him to Sigfredo Garcia, the father of her children, and Garcia's friend Luis Rivera. Prosecutors said Garcia shot Markel while Rivera drove the getaway car. Over the next decade, investigators used cellphone records, surveillance video, financial records and secretly recorded conversations to build the case. "Investigators suspected members of the family were involved, but weren't able to prove it beyond a reasonable doubt for a really long time," Fletcher said. articles.title: Missouri woman federally indicted over chilling death threats sent to Austin Metcalf's family
articles.summary: Sharifa Nicole Henderson faces federal indictment after allegedly sending death threats to Austin Metcalf's family following Karmelo Anthony's conviction.
articles.body: A Missouri woman was federally indicted in Texas after allegedly threatening the family of Austin Metcalf following Karmelo Anthony's conviction for the teenager's killing. Sharifa Nicole Henderson, 34, was arrested in Kansas City on Sept. 11, two days after a federal grand jury in the Eastern District of Texas indicted her on three counts of interstate threatening communications. Anthony's trial concluded on June 9, and prosecutors allege Henderson made three separate death threats against the Metcalf family in the days that followed. On June 10, Henderson sent a message through Facebook Messenger to one of the Metcalf family members saying she would kill them and put them in a body bag before stating, "now this is a threat take me to court [expletive]," according to the indictment. KARMELO ANTHONY SUPPORTER REPORTEDLY FIRED AS OTHER BACKERS FACE BACKLASH OVER VERDICT REMARKS Again on June 10, Henderson called the Collin County government, which prosecuted the case against Anthony, and said she would "demolish" the Metcalf family and "strangle" one of them, per the indictment. And on June 11, prosecutors say Henderson sent another threatening message on Facebook Messenger to a family member. "Don't worry I'll kill you next," she allegedly wrote, according to the indictment. "I will hunt you forever until I kill you...I will be there. You will always have to look over your [expletive] shoulder." If convicted, Henderson faces up to five years in prison for each charge. AUSTIN METCALF'S FATHER ACCUSES MEDIA PUNDITS OF TRYING TO MONETIZE HIS SON'S DEATH 'FOR CLICKS' Jeff Metcalf, Metcalf's father, recently told FOX 4 Dallas-Fort Worth that his family has received more than 100 threats since the end of the murder trial. The case drew national attention and became racially charged, with supporters of Anthony criticizing the lack of Black jurors and calling for his acquittal, while supporters of the Metcalf family gathered outside the courthouse seeking justice. Anthony, 19, was convicted more than a year after fatally stabbing Metcalf, 17, during a regional high school track meet at Kuykendall Stadium in Frisco, Texas, on April 2, 2025. Anthony, then a Centennial High School student, made his way over to the Memorial High School team's tent and sat under it, according to investigators. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Metcalf, a student at Memorial High, then allegedly told Anthony to leave. Prosecutors said Anthony provoked the confrontation that ended with Metcalf being fatally stabbed in the chest. Surveillance footage later released showed Anthony running from the tent. In police reports obtained by Fox News Digital, Anthony was heard telling arresting officers: "I'm not alleged, I did it." Authorities would later say they found no evidence suggesting the two knew each other prior to the incident. A Collin County jury sentenced Anthony to 35 years in prison. Last month, a judge denied Anthony's motion for a new trial, though the family is readying another appeal.

articles.title: NHL top star facing backlash after supporting Putin’s party in Russian elections
articles.summary: Russian NHL hockey star Alex Ovechkin is facing a wave of criticism after appearing in an election ad for Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party.
articles.body: Russian NHL hockey star Alexander Ovechkin is facing a wave of criticism after appearing in an election ad for President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party. A video released ahead of Russia’s parliamentary elections this weekend shows the hockey star endorsing Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who is one of the political heavyweights among the party’s candidates, as Lavrov warns Moscow’s enemies to “expect no mercy.” Ovechkin, who captains the Washington Capitals, said he had felt no hesitation about appearing in the ad. “I’m Russian. I support my country,” he told reporters at a news conference on Thursday, adding that he expects to retire to Russia once his NHL career is over. “I’m gonna live there, my kids are gonna live there. I’m for peace and love and I hope everything’s going to be okay.” The video, and Ovechkin’s subsequent statements, have sparked harsh criticism in Europe, the United States and Canada, which is part of the NHL. Latvia announced on Thursday that it has banned Ovechkin from entering the country. In the same statement, the Latvian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it was also banning Umar Kremlev, the Kremlin-connected businessman who reportedly spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to fund parts of Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding celebration in the Bahamas. President Donald Trump on Friday claimed his son had paid back the Russian billionaire. The Ukrainian Canadian Congress, which represents the roughly 1.3 million Canadians who identify as Ukrainian, called for Ovechkin to be sanctioned and banned from entering Canada, calling him “a disgusting supporter of Russia’s genocidal war against Ukraine.” Meanwhile, Rep. Joe Wilson (R-SC) sent a letter to NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman saying it was “incredibly alarming” that Ovechkin had shown public support for “the party of war criminal Putin.” He called on the league to review its policies. Russia denies allegations that it is committing war crimes in Ukraine despite the charges brought against Putin and other Russian officials by the International Criminal Court. Olga Saladukha, the head of the Ukrainian Athletics Federation, said in a statement the video illustrated why sport and politics cannot be separated when it comes to Russia. “Sport and athletes represent in the Russian Federation – yet another element of the state, state propaganda, militarism and imperial delusions,” she said. And NHL Hall of Fame goaltender Dominik Hasek posted on X that Ovechkin “bears a significant share of responsibility through his public stance… for the hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of Ukrainians and Russians killed or maimed.” ‘A difficult situation’ Alongside Ovechkin, the video features an array of Kremlin propagandists, including the editor-in-chief of state broadcaster RT, Margarita Simonyan, and the film star and staunch Putin supporter Vladimir Mashkov, best known for the 2001 movie “Behind Enemy Lines” and 2011’s “Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol.” Mashkov has been sanctioned in Europe over his backing for Russia’s war in Ukraine. The Washington Capitals said in a statement Ovechkin had been asked to film the video while he was in Russia for the summer. Capitals ⁠general manager ​Chris Patrick told ESPN that Ovechkin had not told the team about the filming. “I would say it’s a difficult situation, and I understand why people are upset,” Patrick was quoted as saying. Ovechkin is one of the NHL’s most decorated players. He has been captain of the Washington Capitals for 16 seasons and had his multi-million contract with the team renewed for another season in July. He became the NHL’s all-time top scorer in April 2025, receiving a personal congratulatory message from Putin. He then scored his record 900th goal last November, a month after turning 40. Ovechkin’s friendship with Putin is no secret – his Instagram profile photo is a snap with the Russian leader and he has previously campaigned for him. But he has adopted a more careful tone since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. He previously said he had “lots of friends in Russia and Ukraine” and hoped the war would be over soon.
